claim: Standard surgery and radiation for glioblastoma gives a median survival of only 12.6 months.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a lethal form of brain cancer with standard surgery and radiation giving a median survival of only 12.6 months (Carlsson et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carlsson et al., 2014.

claim: The addition of temozolomide chemotherapy provides only an additional 2.5 months in the small subset of responsive patients.
source: The addition of temozolomide chemotherapy provides only an additional 2.5 months in the small subset of responsive patients (Stupp et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stupp et al., 2005.

claim: No targeted therapies have been successfully developed for glioblastoma despite extensive characterization and stratification of the bulk primary tumors.
source: Despite extensive characterization and stratification of the bulk primary tumors, no targeted therapies have been successfully developed (Carlsson et al., 2014; von Neubeck et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carlsson et al., 2014 and von Neubeck et al., 2015.

claim: GBM tumors are rooted in self-renewing tumor-initiating cells commonly referred to as glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs).
source: GBM tumors are rooted in self-renewing tumor-initiating cells commonly referred to as glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) (Venere et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venere et al., 2011.

claim: Glioblastoma stem cells drive disease progression in vivo.
source: GBM tumors are rooted in self-renewing tumor-initiating cells commonly referred to as glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) (Venere et al., 2011) that drive disease progression in vivo (Chen et al., 2012; Gallo et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012 and Gallo et al., 2015.

claim: Glioblastoma stem cells display resistance to chemo- and radiotherapy leading to disease recurrence.
source: GBM tumors are rooted in self-renewing tumor-initiating cells commonly referred to as glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) (Venere et al., 2011) that drive disease progression in vivo (Chen et al., 2012; Gallo et al., 2015) and display resistance to chemo- and radiotherapy leading to disease recurrence (Bao et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bao et al., 2006.

claim: Primary GBM consists of four cellular states: neural-progenitor-like (NPC), oligodendrocyte-progenitor-like (OPC), astrocyte-like (AC), and mesenchymal-like (MES).
source: Intratumoral heterogeneity within primary GBM has recently been documented through single-cell RNA-seq experiments and revealed a continuum between four cellular states (Neftel et al., 2019): neural-progenitor-like (NPC), oligodendrocyte-progenitor-like (OPC), astrocyte-like (AC), and mesenchymal-like (MES) (Neftel et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Neftel et al., 2019.

claim: GBM cells lie along a single axis of variation from proneural to mesenchymal transcriptional profiles, with cells expressing stem-associated genes lying at the extremes of this axis.
source: A subsequent study (Wang et al., 2019) using single-cell gene-centric enrichment analysis placed GBM cells along a single axis of variation from proneural to mesenchymal transcriptional profiles, with cells expressing stem-associated genes lying at the extremes of this axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Chromatin accessibility readily discriminates stem from mature cell populations.
source: Chromatin accessibility readily discriminates stem from mature cell populations (Stergachis et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stergachis et al., 2013.

claim: Single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling across four primary adult GBM tumors revealed seven to nine accessibility modules in each tumor based on unsupervised clustering.
source: Applying single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling (scATAC-seq) across four primary adult GBM tumors (3797 cells), wild type for both IDH1 and IDH2, revealed seven to nine accessibility modules in each tumor based on unsupervised clustering (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from scATAC-seq experiments and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: Across the four tumors, 35–55.2% of the cells were significantly enriched for at least one state's signature genes.
source: Across the four tumors, 35–55.2% of the cells were significantly enriched for at least one state's signature genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The MES state dominates the identity of two or more modules reported from chromatin accessibility in every tumor.
source: The MES state reported from scRNA-seq (Neftel et al., 2019) dominates the identity of two or more modules reported from chromatin accessibility in every tumor (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The NPC and OPC states are mixed within the same module defined based on chromatin accessibility, dominating over the other states typically in at least two modules.
source: In contrast, the NPC and OPC states are mixed within the same module defined based on chromatin accessibility, dominating over the other states typically in at least two modules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the chromatin accessibility analysis described in the text.

claim: Cells assigned to the AC state did not preferentially cluster within a single module reported from chromatin accessibility.
source: Cells assigned to the AC state did not preferentially cluster within a single module reported from chromatin accessibility (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Chromatin accessibility reflects a greater stratification of the MES state and detects similarities between the OPC and NPC states and heterogeneity within the AC state.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that chromatin accessibility reflects a greater stratification of the MES state and detects similarities between the OPC and NPC states and heterogeneity within the AC state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the chromatin accessibility analysis results described in the text.

claim: Individual cells scoring as putative cancer stem cells were not restricted to a unique module defined by chromatin accessibility but were distributed across a subset of modules.
source: Individual cells scoring as putative cancer stem cells were not restricted to a unique module defined by chromatin accessibility but were distributed across a subset of modules, suggesting heterogeneity across cancer stem cells in primary GBM, in agreement with reports relying on single GBM cell labeling (Corces et al., 2016; Gallo et al., 2015; Lan et al., 2017; Liau et al., 2017; Meyer et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2017; Orzan et al., 2017; Park et al., 2017; Rheinbay et al., 2013; Stergachis et al., 2013; Suvà et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and citations to multiple previous reports.

claim: Putative cancer stem cells identified in primary GBM through scATAC-seq were found in modules ascribed to every one of the four cellular states defined by gene expression, predominantly within NPC and OPC containing modules and a smaller fraction (<10%) in MES-specific modules across all four tumors.
source: Putative cancer stem cells identified in primary GBM through scATAC-seq were found in modules ascribed to every one of the four cellular states defined by gene expression (Neftel et al., 2019), predominantly within NPC and OPC containing modules and a smaller fraction (<10%) in MES-specific modules across all four tumors (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The core transcriptional unit of cancer stem cells in primary GBM is not restricted to a unique population defined by its global transcriptional or chromatin accessibility profile with the resolution achieved with current single-cell technologies.
source: This suggests that the core transcriptional unit of cancer stem cells in primary GBM (Suvà et al., 2014) is not restricted to a unique population defined by its global transcriptional or chromatin accessibility profile with the resolution achieved with current single-cell technologies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data and supported by a citation to Suvà et al., 2014.

claim: Each patient-derived GSC showed a similar enrichment for accessible chromatin regions in promoters and 5′UTRs, and depletion in introns and distal intergenic regions.
source: Each patient-derived GSC showed a similar enrichment for accessible chromatin regions in promoters and 5′UTRs, and depletion in introns and distal intergenic regions (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: 92% of the total predicted regions of accessible chromatin (255,891 regions) within GSCs were uncovered based on a saturation analysis using a self-starting non-linear regression model across the 27 samples.
source: Collectively, we uncovered 92% of the total predicted regions of accessible chromatin (255,891 regions) within GSCs based on a saturation analysis using a self-starting non-linear regression model across the 27 samples (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from saturation analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: On average, 11.3% of cells in each primary GBM were labeled as GSCs.
source: On average, 11.3% of cells in each primary GBM were labeled as GSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the GSC identification analysis.

claim: The enrichment z-scores for both cancer stem signatures (i.e. stem transcription factors signature and GSC chromatin accessibility signature) are significantly correlated across cells in all four tumors (p≤1.6×10−5).
source: Moreover, the enrichment z-scores for both cancer stem signatures (i.e. stem transcription factors signature and GSC chromatin accessibility signature) are significantly correlated across cells in all four tumors (p≤1.6×10−5) (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: The overlap in cells significantly enriched for either stem signatures across the four tumors is significant (hypergeometric test p-value=8.8×10−8).
source: The overlap in cells significantly enriched for either stem signatures across the four tumors is also significant (hypergeometric test p-value=8.8×10−8)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using a hypergeometric test.

claim: An average of 91.2% (85.1–100%) of the cells identified by either signature display the hallmark GBM copy number changes at chromosomes 7 and 10, confirming their neoplastic status.
source: Additionally, an average of 91.2% (85.1–100%) of the cells identified by either signature display the hallmark GBM copy number changes at chromosomes 7 and 10, confirming their neoplastic status (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by copy number analysis data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patient-derived GSC populations reflect the chromatin identity of putative cancer stem cells found in primary brain tumors.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that the patient-derived GSC populations reflect the chromatin identity of putative cancer stem cells found in primary brain tumors, highlighting the value of these GSCs as models to deepen our understanding of individual cells within primary GBM with features found in self-renewing tumor-initiating cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the concordance between GSC signatures and cancer stem cells in primary tumors.

claim: Spectral clustering of the 27 patient-derived GSC ATAC profiles identifies three distinct states of self-renewing tumor-initiating cells.
source: Accordingly, spectral clustering of the 27 patient-derived GSC ATAC profiles identifies three distinct states of self-renewing tumor-initiating cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by spectral clustering analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression profiling of the 27 GSCs by RNA-seq reveals GSCs significantly enriched for the signatures of each of the three TCGA GBM subtypes (proneural, classical, and mesenchymal).
source: Expression profiling of these 27 GSCs by RNA-seq reveals GSCs significantly enriched for the signatures of each of the three TCGA GBM subtypes (proneural, classical, and mesenchymal) (Wang et al., 2017; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citation to Wang et al., 2017, presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The assignment of the proneural, classical, and mesenchymal subtypes across GSCs did not match the three clusters identified from ATAC-seq.
source: However, the assignment of the proneural, classical, and mesenchymal subtypes across GSCs did not match the three clusters identified from ATAC-seq (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Clustering the GSCs by gene expression, independently of their chromatin accessibility, did largely recapitulate the GSC states defined by chromatin accessibility.
source: Conversely, clustering the GSCs by gene expression, independently of their chromatin accessibility, did largely recapitulate the GSC states defined by chromatin accessibility (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The largest GSC state is a Reactive state, with terms related to immune cells and response.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis with GSEA (Gene Set Enrichment Analysis) (Subramanian et al., 2005) and g:profiler (Reimand et al., 2016) using genes exclusively enriched for both expression and promoter chromatin accessibility in each subtype reported significantly enriched terms defining the largest GSC state as a Reactive state, with terms related to immune cells and response (Figure 3C, top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis and presented in Figure 3C.

claim: A second GSC state was enriched for Constructive gene sets involved in brain, neuron, and glial cell development.
source: A second GSC state was enriched for Constructive gene sets involved in brain, neuron, and glial cell development (Figure 3C, middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis and presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The third and smallest GSC state presented an Invasive state characterized by terms relating to the extracellular matrix and angiogenesis.
source: The third and smallest GSC state presented an Invasive state characterized by terms relating to the extracellular matrix and angiogenesis (Figure 3C, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis and presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The CNA-based classification of GSCs failed to match the three chromatin accessibility-derived states, suggesting the three GSC states are not defined by somatic copy number events.
source: While common GBM CNAs, including EGFR gains and CDKN2A/B loss, were observed, the CNA-based classification of GSCs failed to match the three chromatin accessibility-derived states, suggesting the three GSC states are not defined by somatic copy number events (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by copy number analysis presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Only a small subset of accessible chromatin regions drives the three GSC states.
source: Further comparison of the accessible chromatin in each GSC state reveals that only a small subset of accessible chromatin regions drives the three GSC states (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis presented in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The comprehensiveness of the cohort saturated the detection of accessible regions to 93%, 88%, and 71% across the Reactive (n = 13), Constructive (n = 9), and Invasive (n = 5) state GSCs, respectively.
source: Our ability to discriminate GSC state-specific regions of accessible chromatin is reflective of the comprehensiveness of our cohort to saturate the detection of accessible regions to 93%, 88%, and 71% across the Reactive (n = 13), Constructive (n = 9), and Invasive (n = 5) state GSCs, respectively (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by saturation analysis presented in Figure 3F.

claim: The DNA recognition motifs for the interferon-regulatory factor (IRF) and Cys2-His2 zinc finger (C2H2 ZF) transcription factor families were enriched in the Reactive state.
source: Specifically, the DNA recognition motifs for the interferon-regulatory factor (IRF) and Cys2-His2 zinc finger (C2H2 ZF) transcription factor families were enriched in the Reactive state (Figure 4A, top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Regulatory factor X (RFX) and basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) DNA recognition motifs were enriched in the Constructive state.
source: Regulatory factor X (RFX) and basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) DNA recognition motifs were enriched in the Constructive state (Figure 4A, middle panel)
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The Forkhead motif family was enriched in the Invasive state.
source: while the Forkhead motif family was enriched in the Invasive state (Figure 4A, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The SP1 regulatory network is preferentially essential in the Reactive state GSCs.
source: Specifically, the SP1 regulatory network is preferentially essential in the Reactive state GSCs (Figure 4B, top panel)
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR/Cas9 essentiality screen data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: ASCL1, OLIG2, AHR, and NPAS3 are uniquely essential in the Constructive state GSCs.
source: ASCL1, OLIG2, AHR, and NPAS3 are uniquely essential in the Constructive state GSCs (Figure 4B, middle panel)
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR/Cas9 essentiality screen data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: FOXD1 is essential only in the Invasive state GSC.
source: and FOXD1 is essential only in the Invasive state GSC (Figure 4B, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR/Cas9 essentiality screen data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Of the 36 transcription factors from the Reactive-enriched families (IRF and C2H2 ZF) that were essential in at least one Reactive GSC and not in any of the Constructive or Invasive GSCs, 13 are directly regulated by SP1.
source: However, of the 36 transcription factors from the Reactive-enriched families (IRF and C2H2 ZF) that were essential in at least one Reactive GSC and not in any of the Constructive or Invasive GSCs, 13 are directly regulated by SP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of transcription factor regulation presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All six key transcription factors (SP1, ASCL1, OLIG2, AHR, NPAS3, FOXD1) display significantly higher expression in GBM compared to normal brain.
source: Notably, all six transcription factors display significantly higher expression in GBM compared to normal brain (Tang et al., 2017; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from Tang et al., 2017 and presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Constructive state was dominant in every primary tumor, ranging from 9 to 21% of all cells captured by scATAC-seq.
source: The Constructive state was dominant in every primary tumor, ranging from 9 to 21% of all cells captured by scATAC-seq (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scATAC-seq data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The Reactive and Invasive states accounted for only 0–9% of all cells, in varying proportions from one tumor to another.
source: The Reactive and Invasive states accounted for only 0–9% of all cells, in varying proportions from one tumor to another (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scATAC-seq data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The overall survival times of mice transplanted with GSCs grouped by GSC state were significantly different (LogRank test p=0.041).
source: The overall survival times of the transplanted mice grouped by GSC state were significantly different (LogRank test p=0.041), with the Invasive state GSCs leading to the worst prognosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of xenograft survival data.

claim: Relative to the mice injected with Reactive state GSCs, mice with Constructive state GSCs and Invasive state GSCs had hazard ratios of 1.3 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.57–2.97) and 3.5 (95% CI: 1.2–10.49), respectively.
source: Relative to the mice injected with Reactive state GSCs, mice with Constructive state GSCs and Invasive state GSCs had hazard ratios of 1.3 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.57–2.97) and 3.5 (95% CI: 1.2–10.49), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of xenograft survival data.

claim: GSCs of the Invasive state invaded strikingly faster and further into the collagen matrix and overall displayed a three times greater invasive ability than that of the Reactive and Constructive states.
source: GSCs of the Invasive state invaded strikingly faster and further into the collagen matrix and overall displayed a three times greater invasive ability than that of the Reactive and Constructive states.
evidence: The claim is supported by invasion assay data.

claim: An Invasive-high subset of TCGA tumors has significantly lower survival (p=0.019, HR (Hazard Ratio) = 2.8, 95% CI: [1.3–5.81]).
source: With this stratification method, median patient survival per group not only decreased with increasing Invasive GSC score, but we also identified an Invasive-high subset of tumors with significantly lower survival (p=0.019, HR (Hazard Ratio) = 2.8, 95% CI: [1.3–5.81]) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis of TCGA data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Cancer stem cell states defined based on the chromatin accessibility in GSCs can identify transcriptional programs associated with poor prognosis and can serve as a signature to identify high-risk patients in IDH wild-type GBM.
source: These results show that cancer stem cell states defined based on the chromatin accessibility in GSCs can identify transcriptional programs associated with poor prognosis and can serve as a signature to identify high-risk patients in IDH wild-type GBM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the survival analysis results.

claim: Chromatin accessibility assays capture a heterogeneity across self-renewing tumor-initiating cells in primary GBM that extends beyond their genetic diversity and underlies the heterogeneity in bulk progeny.
source: Here we show that chromatin accessibility assays capture a heterogeneity across self-renewing tumor-initiating cells in primary GBM that extends beyond their genetic diversity and underlies the heterogeneity in bulk progeny (Meyer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings and a citation to Meyer et al., 2015.

claim: This heterogeneity aligns with diversity in the three-dimensional genome organization of GSCs.
source: This heterogeneity aligns with diversity in the three-dimensional genome organization of GSCs (Johnston et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnston et al., 2019.

claim: The three-dimensional genome organization instructs cis-regulatory plexuses underlying gene regulation.
source: and agrees with how the three-dimensional genome organization instructs cis-regulatory plexuses underlying gene regulation (Bailey et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2016; Sallari et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2016; Zheng and Xie, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The Invasive GSC signature draws from a population with enhanced ability to invade and spread compared to other GSC states.
source: Specifically, the Invasive GSC signature draws from a population with enhanced ability to invade and spread compared to other GSC states.
evidence: The claim is supported by invasion assay data.

claim: SP1 and its regulatory partners are involved in cellular differentiation and growth, apoptosis, response to DNA damage, chromatin remodeling.
source: Specifically, the Reactive GSC state-associated transcription factor SP1 and its regulatory partners are involved in cellular differentiation and growth, apoptosis, response to DNA damage, chromatin remodeling (O'Connor et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Connor et al., 2016.

claim: SP1 is involved in stimulation of TERT expression in cancer stem cells.
source: stimulation of TERT expression in cancer stem cells (Liu et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: SP1 is involved in increased stemness and invasion in GBM.
source: and increased stemness and invasion in GBM (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2014.

claim: OLIG2 is a known GSC marker.
source: In contrast, the Constructive GSC state relies on transcription factors including OLIG2, a known GSC marker (Trépant et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Trépant et al., 2015.

claim: AHR is involved in tumor microenvironment responses and metabolic adaptation.
source: AHR involved in tumor microenvironment responses and metabolic adaptation (Gabriely et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gabriely et al., 2017.

claim: NPAS3 is a regulator of Notch signaling and neurogenesis.
source: NPAS3, a regulator of Notch signaling and neurogenesis (Michaelson et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Michaelson et al., 2017.

claim: ASCL1 is a critical regulator of GSC differentiation and marker of sensitivity to Notch inhibition in GSCs.
source: and ASCL1, a critical regulator of GSC differentiation and marker of sensitivity to Notch inhibition in GSCs (Park et al., 2017; Rajakulendran et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2017 and Rajakulendran et al., 2019.

claim: FOXD1 is a pluripotency regulator and determinant of tumorigenicity in GSCs regulating expression of the aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH1A3, a functional marker for invasive GSCs.
source: Finally, the Invasive GSC state relies on FOXD1, a pluripotency regulator and determinant of tumorigenicity in GSCs regulating expression of the aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH1A3, a functional marker for invasive GSCs (Cheng et al., 2016; Koga et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2016 and Koga et al., 2014.

claim: Primary human GBMs harbor a heterogeneous self-renewing population whose diversity is captured in patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs).
source: We show, using single-cell chromatin accessibility, that primary human GBMs harbor a heterogeneous self-renewing population whose diversity is captured in patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's single-cell chromatin accessibility data.

claim: In-depth characterization of chromatin accessibility in GSCs identifies three GSC states: Reactive, Constructive, and Invasive, each governed by uniquely essential transcription factors and present within GBMs in varying proportions.
source: In-depth characterization of chromatin accessibility in GSCs identifies three GSC states: Reactive, Constructive, and Invasive, each governed by uniquely essential transcription factors and present within GBMs in varying proportions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's chromatin accessibility and essentiality screen data.

claim: GSC states associate with survival in orthotopic xenografts.
source: Orthotopic xenografts reveal that GSC states associate with survival
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft survival data.

claim: An invasive GSC signature is predictive of low patient survival.
source: and identify an invasive GSC signature predictive of low patient survival
evidence: The claim is supported by TCGA survival analysis data.

claim: Invasive state GSCs have higher invasive properties compared to Reactive and Constructive GSCs as shown by in vitro and in vivo assays.
source: in line with the higher invasive properties of Invasive state GSCs compared to Reactive and Constructive GSCs as shown by in vitro and in vivo assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by invasion assay and xenograft data.
